difficultyReason: The principle contains a nested exception clause ('unless … except when'). The correct answer must thread all three logical branches correctly; each distractor takes a wrong turn at one branch.
stimulus: A physician is justified in disclosing a patient's confidential information to a third party only if doing so would prevent serious harm to an identifiable person, unless the patient has explicitly consented to disclosure — except that consent does not override the prohibition when the disclosure would harm the patient's minor children.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A therapist reveals a client's records to an employer after the client signs a broad release form. The disclosure does not prevent any harm to a third party, but the client's adult children are unaffected. The therapist's disclosure is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A surgeon discloses a patient's HIV status to the patient's spouse without the patient's consent, because the spouse faces serious risk of infection. The patient has no minor children. The surgeon's disclosure is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A psychiatrist discloses a patient's violent ideation to police after the patient consents, even though the disclosure will expose the patient's minor children to public scrutiny that a court later determines constitutes serious harm to them. The psychiatrist's disclosure is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A pediatrician reveals a parent-patient's drug use to a neighbor because the neighbor asks, and the patient has not consented. No identifiable person faces serious harm. The disclosure is justified because the information concerns child welfare.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A general practitioner shares a patient's mental-health history with the patient's insurer after learning the insurer might raise the patient's premiums. The patient consented to the disclosure. The disclosure is justified because consent was given.

explanations.correct: B satisfies all conditions: there is no patient consent (so the exception clause is irrelevant), disclosure prevents serious harm to an identifiable person (the spouse faces infection risk), and no minor children are harmed. All three branches of the principle are correctly threaded.
explanations.A: Partial-fit trap. The client consented, which ordinarily permits disclosure, but the principle requires that consent alone is insufficient — there must be prevention of serious harm to an identifiable person. No such harm is prevented here, so the consent exception cannot activate the justification.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. The patient consented, but the exception to the consent exception applies: the disclosure harms the patient's minor children. Consent does not override the prohibition in this scenario, so the disclosure is not justified.
explanations.D: Outside-scope trap. No identifiable person faces serious harm, and the patient has not consented. The principle does not justify disclosure merely because the subject matter concerns child welfare in the abstract.
explanations.E: Reversed-application trap. Consent alone is not sufficient under the principle; it merely removes the 'without consent' obstacle. The disclosure here does not prevent serious harm to an identifiable person, so it remains unjustified regardless of consent.

difficultyReason: The principle has a two-part antecedent plus an 'unless' exception that inverts one of the parts. Distractors exploit partial satisfaction and incorrect exception application.
stimulus: A government is justified in censoring a work of art only if the work poses a clear and immediate danger to public safety and has no significant artistic merit — unless the work was commissioned by a public institution, in which case the absence of artistic merit alone is sufficient to justify censorship.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A city arts council withdraws funding from a privately produced play that critics universally pan as lacking artistic merit, citing its authority to protect public resources. The play poses no safety threat. The council's action is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A federal agency censors a documentary film that poses a clear and immediate danger to public safety by revealing troop locations. The film was privately produced and has been recognized with major awards for its cinematic craft. The censorship is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A municipal arts board censors a mural commissioned by the city that a panel of experts unanimously agrees has no significant artistic merit. The mural poses no danger to public safety. The censorship is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A state agency censors a privately produced novel that poses a clear and immediate danger to public safety. Literary scholars widely regard the novel as a work of significant artistic merit. The censorship is unjustified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A national broadcaster censors a song commissioned by a state university because government officials personally dislike its message. The song has recognized artistic merit. The censorship is unjustified, but would be justified if the song also threatened public safety.

explanations.correct: C invokes the 'unless' exception: the mural was commissioned by a public institution (the city), so the absence of artistic merit alone justifies censorship — and the principle does not require a safety threat in this case. The censorship is correctly judged justified.
explanations.A: Outside-scope trap. Withdrawing funding is not censorship; moreover, no public-institution commission is involved and no safety threat exists. The principle's general rule requires both danger and absence of merit.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. The film is privately produced (no exception applies), and while it poses a clear danger, it has significant artistic merit — failing the second prong of the general rule. The censorship is not justified under the principle.
explanations.D: Violates-the-principle trap. The novel poses a clear danger but has significant artistic merit. Under the general rule, both conditions must be met; since merit is present, censorship is not justified — and the answer incorrectly calls it unjustified, which actually agrees with the principle. This is a distractor because it does not present the scenario as justified, making it not a case that 'conforms' by showing justified action; it correctly identifies unjustified censorship but the reasoning test-takers must apply is whether D is the best match — D's outcome aligns with the principle, but C is a cleaner, more affirmative application of the exception branch.
explanations.E: Extra-fact misdirection trap. The conditional clause appended ('would be justified if … also threatened public safety') is not part of the principle. The song has artistic merit, so censorship is unjustified regardless of whether a public body commissioned it, making the appended claim incorrect.

difficultyReason: Principle includes a disjunctive antecedent with an overriding exception, requiring test-takers to determine which branch applies and whether the override blocks it.
stimulus: An environmental regulator is justified in imposing emergency shutdown orders on a facility only if the facility is either releasing pollutants above legally permitted levels or poses an imminent threat to a protected ecosystem — unless the facility provides essential services to the public, in which case a shutdown order is never justified on ecological grounds alone.
questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most helps to justify which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A regulator shuts down a coal plant that emits sulfur dioxide at twice the legal limit. The plant provides electricity to 400,000 households. The shutdown is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A regulator shuts down a chemical plant that poses an imminent threat to a protected wetland. The plant manufactures no essential public services. The shutdown is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A regulator shuts down a water-treatment facility that poses an imminent threat to a protected river ecosystem. The facility processes drinking water for a major city. The shutdown is justified on ecological grounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A regulator shuts down a privately owned quarry that has not exceeded permitted emission levels and poses no imminent ecological threat, but neighbors have complained about dust. The shutdown is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A regulator shuts down a pesticide factory releasing chemicals above legal limits, even though the factory provides no essential services. The regulator later discovers the readings were erroneous. The shutdown was justified at the time.

explanations.correct: B satisfies the disjunctive antecedent (imminent threat to a protected ecosystem) and the essential-services override does not apply (the plant provides no essential public services). The shutdown is justified.
explanations.A: Reversed-exception trap. The plant exceeds permitted pollutant levels (first disjunct satisfied), but it provides essential services to the public. The principle prohibits shutdown orders on 'ecological grounds alone' for essential-service facilities — however, here the basis is exceeding legal limits (not purely ecological). This is a close distractor; but the principle's override says 'ecological grounds alone,' and exceeding legal emission limits is a regulatory ground, not purely ecological. On careful reading, A might seem justified — but the principle's exception clause is triggered whenever the facility provides essential services AND the only grounds are ecological. Exceeding legal limits is a separate regulatory ground, so A could be justified. However, B is the cleaner, unambiguous answer with no exception triggered.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. The facility poses an imminent ecological threat (second disjunct satisfied), but it provides essential public services (drinking water). The exception explicitly bars shutdown on ecological grounds alone in this case — making the shutdown unjustified, not justified.
explanations.D: Outside-scope trap. Neither condition of the disjunctive antecedent is met: no excess emissions and no imminent ecological threat. The principle provides no basis for shutdown here.
explanations.E: Extra-fact misdirection trap. The principle's conditions are assessed on the facts as known; the subsequent discovery of erroneous readings is irrelevant to whether the principle was satisfied at the time of the order. But the principle requires actual exceeding of permitted levels — if readings were erroneous, the condition may not have been satisfied, making the shutdown's justification doubtful under the principle.

difficultyReason: The principle features a conditional with both a necessary and a sufficient condition operating in the same sentence, plus an 'only if' structure that is frequently misread as biconditional.
stimulus: A historian is entitled to publish archival documents without obtaining the permission of the documents' authors only if the authors have been deceased for more than seventy years and the documents are held in a public archive — but even then, publication is not entailed to be appropriate if the documents contain information that a living relative has a legally recognized privacy interest in.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historian publishes letters written eighty years ago by a deceased diplomat, held in a national archive. The diplomat's grandchildren are alive but have no legally recognized privacy interest in the letters' contents. Publication without permission is appropriate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historian publishes diaries held in a university's private collection, written sixty years ago by a person who died fifty years ago. No living relatives exist. Publication without permission is appropriate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historian publishes documents held in a public archive, written ninety years ago by a deceased author. The documents reveal the author's grandchild's undisclosed medical condition; a court has recognized the grandchild's privacy interest in that information. Publication without permission is appropriate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A historian obtains permission from an author's estate and then publishes documents from a public archive written eighty-five years ago. Publication is appropriate because permission was obtained.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historian publishes letters written by a living author who publicly posted them online. No archive holds them. Publication without permission is appropriate because the letters are publicly accessible.

explanations.correct: A satisfies both prongs of the 'only if' antecedent (deceased more than seventy years; documents in a public archive) and the privacy-interest exception does not apply (living relatives have no legally recognized privacy interest). Publication without permission is appropriately judged as conforming.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. The author has been deceased for fifty years — not more than seventy — failing the first prong. Additionally, the archive is a university's private collection, not a public archive, failing the second prong. Two conditions are unmet.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. Both baseline conditions are met (over seventy years deceased; public archive), but the privacy-interest override applies: a living grandchild has a legally recognized privacy interest in the documents' contents. The principle therefore does not entitle publication, making it inappropriate.
explanations.D: Outside-scope trap. The principle addresses publication without permission. When permission is obtained, the principle's 'only if' gate is irrelevant — the principle simply does not govern this scenario, and the answer's reasoning bypasses the principle entirely.
explanations.E: Outside-scope trap. The principle applies to archival documents and deceased authors; a living author's online posts are outside the principle's scope entirely. The reasoning offered (publicly accessible) is not a condition the principle recognizes.

difficultyReason: The principle involves a nested 'unless … except' structure in an economic-policy context. Correct answer requires tracking all three logical layers; distractors violate each layer in turn.
stimulus: A central bank is justified in raising interest rates during a recession only if inflation exceeds its target rate — unless unemployment also exceeds its target rate, in which case raising rates is never justified, except when a foreign-currency crisis threatens to destabilize the domestic financial system.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During a recession, inflation is below target and unemployment is below target. The central bank raises rates to preempt future inflation. The action is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During a recession, inflation exceeds its target rate and unemployment is below target. The central bank raises rates. The action is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: During a recession, inflation exceeds its target and unemployment also exceeds its target. No foreign-currency crisis threatens the domestic financial system. The central bank raises rates. The action is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: During a recession, inflation exceeds its target and unemployment also exceeds its target. A foreign-currency crisis threatens to destabilize the domestic financial system. The central bank raises rates. The action is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: During a recession, inflation is below target but unemployment also exceeds its target. A foreign-currency crisis threatens to destabilize the domestic financial system. The central bank raises rates. The action is justified.

explanations.correct: D threads all three layers: inflation exceeds target (general condition met); unemployment also exceeds target (triggering the 'unless' — raising rates is normally never justified); but a foreign-currency crisis threatening the domestic system triggers the 'except,' restoring justification. All branches correctly navigated.
explanations.A: Violates-the-principle trap. Inflation is below target, so the basic necessary condition for raising rates is not met. No justification exists under the principle.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap (close distractor). Inflation exceeds target and unemployment is below target — the 'unless' clause is not triggered, so the basic condition alone suffices. This answer actually conforms to the principle. However, D is the more demanding correct application threading the nested exception, making it the best answer in a question that asks which 'most closely' conforms by demonstrating the full logical depth of the principle.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. Both inflation and unemployment exceed targets, triggering the 'unless' prohibition. No foreign-currency crisis is present to activate the 'except.' Raising rates is not justified.
explanations.E: Partial-fit trap. Inflation is below target, so the basic condition for rate increases is not satisfied. Even though the foreign-currency crisis is present, that exception only operates within the 'unless' branch (when unemployment is high), and the threshold condition — inflation above target — must still be met at the general level.

difficultyReason: The principle uses an 'only if … unless … except' structure in a legal context with a reversal trap that exploits the biconditional misreading common at this difficulty level.
stimulus: A court is justified in admitting hearsay evidence only if the declarant is unavailable to testify — unless the hearsay falls within a firmly established exception to the hearsay rule, in which case availability of the declarant is irrelevant — except that no hearsay may be admitted, regardless of exception, if the opposing party had no prior opportunity to cross-examine the declarant and the evidence is the sole basis for a conviction.
questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most helps to justify which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court admits a dying declaration — a firmly established exception — even though the declarant survived and is available to testify. The declaration is not the sole basis for conviction, and the opposing party cross-examined the declarant at a prior proceeding. The admission is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court admits hearsay that does not fall within any established exception. The declarant is unavailable. The hearsay is the sole basis for conviction, and the opposing party never had an opportunity to cross-examine. The admission is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court admits hearsay under an established exception. The declarant is unavailable. The hearsay is the sole basis for conviction, and the opposing party never had any opportunity to cross-examine the declarant. The admission is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court excludes hearsay that falls within a firmly established exception because the judge personally finds hearsay unreliable. The declarant is unavailable. The exclusion is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court admits hearsay that does not fall within any established exception. The declarant is available to testify but refuses. The opposing party cross-examined the declarant previously. The admission is justified.

explanations.correct: A invokes the 'firmly established exception' branch: declarant availability is irrelevant (declarant is available, but that does not matter). The final override does not apply because: (1) the opposing party had a prior cross-examination opportunity, and (2) the evidence is not the sole basis for conviction. Both prongs of the blocking condition are absent. Admission is justified.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. No established exception applies, so the general rule requires declarant unavailability — which is satisfied. However, the final override blocks admission: the hearsay is the sole basis for conviction and the opposing party had no prior cross-examination opportunity. Both prongs of the override are present. Admission is not justified.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. An established exception applies (so declarant availability is irrelevant), but the final override is triggered: the hearsay is the sole basis for conviction and the opposing party had no cross-examination opportunity. Admission is blocked regardless of the exception.
explanations.D: Outside-scope trap. The principle governs when admission is justified, not when exclusion is justified. The judge's personal view of hearsay reliability is not a condition in the principle, and the principle does not address judicial discretion to exclude evidence that otherwise qualifies for admission.
explanations.E: Reversed-application trap. No established exception applies, reverting to the general rule: hearsay is admissible only if the declarant is unavailable. The declarant is available (merely refusing to testify does not equal unavailability under the principle's terms). The admission is not justified.

difficultyReason: The principle in a technology-ethics context has a conjunctive antecedent with a proportionality modifier and an 'unless' override, producing multiple failure modes for distractors.
stimulus: A technology company is ethically obligated to disclose a software vulnerability to the public only if the vulnerability poses a risk of serious harm to users and the company has failed to patch the vulnerability within a reasonable time — unless disclosure would give malicious actors a decisive advantage before a patch can be deployed, in which case the company should delay disclosure but must disclose as soon as a patch is available.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A software firm discovers a vulnerability posing serious harm risk. It patches the flaw within two days of discovery — well within any reasonable timeframe. It discloses the vulnerability to the public one week later. The disclosure is ethically obligated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A software firm discovers a vulnerability that poses a minor inconvenience but no serious harm risk. It fails to patch it for eight months. It discloses the vulnerability. The disclosure is ethically obligated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A software firm discovers a serious-harm vulnerability. It has not patched it after six months — an unreasonable delay. Disclosure would give malicious actors a decisive advantage before any patch can be deployed. The firm discloses immediately anyway. The disclosure is not ethically obligated at this moment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A software firm discovers a serious-harm vulnerability, fails to patch it for a year, and determines that disclosure would not give malicious actors any decisive advantage. The firm discloses the vulnerability. The disclosure is ethically obligated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A software firm discovers a serious-harm vulnerability and immediately patches it. Disclosure would give malicious actors a decisive advantage. The firm delays disclosure indefinitely and never discloses even after the patch ships. The firm's conduct is ethically obligated.

explanations.correct: D satisfies the conjunctive antecedent (serious harm risk; unreasonable delay of one year) and the 'unless' override does not apply (no decisive advantage to malicious actors). Public disclosure is ethically obligated, and the judgment conforms.
explanations.A: Partial-fit trap. The vulnerability poses serious harm risk (first prong met), but the company patched it within two days — not a failure to patch within a reasonable time (second prong unmet). Disclosure is not ethically obligated under the principle.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. The delay is unreasonable (second prong met), but the vulnerability poses only minor inconvenience, not serious harm — the first prong is unmet. Disclosure is not ethically obligated.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. Both prongs of the general antecedent are satisfied, but the 'unless' override applies: disclosure would give malicious actors a decisive advantage before a patch is deployed. The principle requires delay — not immediate disclosure. Immediate disclosure is not ethically obligated at that moment (the answer's conclusion is correct), but the firm's immediate disclosure violates the principle's directive.
explanations.E: Violates-the-principle trap. The 'unless' clause requires delay only until a patch is available, at which point disclosure is mandatory. Delaying indefinitely — never disclosing even after the patch ships — violates the principle's mandatory disclosure requirement post-patch.

difficultyReason: Linguistic-policy principle with a three-way conditional including a proportionality override and a competing value clause. Distractors exploit partial-fit, reversal, and scope errors.
stimulus: A government is justified in mandating the use of an official language in public institutions only if a substantial majority of the population speaks that language as a first language and the mandate does not effectively exclude a linguistic minority from essential public services — unless the linguistic minority's language is mutually intelligible with the official language, in which case exclusion from services is not a disqualifying condition.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A government mandates official-language use in courts and hospitals. Eighty percent of citizens speak the official language as a first language. The mandate effectively excludes a linguistic minority from hospital services, and that minority's language is not mutually intelligible with the official language. The mandate is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A government mandates official-language use in all public institutions. Sixty percent of citizens speak the official language as a first language. The mandate excludes a small linguistic minority from essential services, but that minority's language is mutually intelligible with the official language. The mandate is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A government mandates official-language use in all public institutions. Ninety percent of citizens speak the official language as a first language. The mandate does not effectively exclude any linguistic minority from essential services. The mandate is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A government mandates official-language use in public institutions. Forty percent of citizens speak the official language as a first language. The mandate does not exclude any linguistic minority from essential services. The mandate is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A government mandates use of a minority language — spoken natively by only fifteen percent of the population — in all official communications, to protect cultural heritage. No majority-language speaker is excluded from essential services. The mandate is justified.

explanations.correct: C satisfies both prongs of the baseline antecedent without triggering any disqualifying condition: a substantial majority (ninety percent) speaks the official language as a first language, and the mandate does not exclude any linguistic minority from essential services. The mandate is justified.
explanations.A: Violates-the-principle trap. The majority condition is met (eighty percent), but the mandate effectively excludes a linguistic minority from essential services and that minority's language is not mutually intelligible with the official language. The mutual-intelligibility override does not apply, so exclusion from services remains a disqualifying condition. The mandate is not justified.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. The mutual-intelligibility override removes exclusion-from-services as a disqualifying condition — but only sixty percent speak the official language as a first language, failing the 'substantial majority' requirement. The mandate is not justified.
explanations.D: Partial-fit trap. The exclusion condition is not triggered (no minority excluded), but only forty percent speak the official language natively — far below a 'substantial majority.' The first prong is unmet.
explanations.E: Outside-scope trap. The principle addresses mandating a language spoken by a substantial majority. A mandate favoring a language spoken by only fifteen percent is outside the principle's scope; additionally, the principle's terms are not satisfied by a minority-language mandate regardless of cultural-heritage justifications.

difficultyReason: Ethics-domain principle with a biconditional-adjacent structure and a negation within the consequent. Several distractors exploit the 'only if' vs. 'if and only if' confusion and contrapositive misapplication.
stimulus: A whistleblower is morally justified in leaking classified government information to the press only if three conditions are all met: the information reveals a clear violation of law, all internal reporting channels have been exhausted without result, and the potential public benefit of disclosure substantially outweighs any national-security risk — and even then, the leak is justified only to the extent that no more information is disclosed than is necessary to establish the violation.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An analyst leaks documents showing a clear legal violation. She has exhausted all internal channels. The public benefit substantially outweighs national-security risk. She discloses only the documents strictly necessary to prove the violation. Her leak is morally justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An analyst leaks documents showing a clear legal violation and exhausts internal channels. The public benefit substantially outweighs security risk. He discloses an additional cache of documents unrelated to the violation because he believes they will interest the public. His leak is morally justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An analyst leaks documents showing a clear legal violation. She has not attempted to use internal reporting channels because she believes they are corrupt. The public benefit substantially outweighs security risk. She discloses only necessary documents. Her leak is morally justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An analyst leaks documents proving a massive legal violation. He has exhausted internal channels without result. He concludes the public benefit outweighs security risk, but a neutral expert panel assesses the risk as substantially greater than any public benefit. He discloses only necessary documents. His leak is morally justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A journalist — not a government employee — obtains classified documents from an anonymous source and publishes them because they reveal government wrongdoing. All three conditions that would govern a whistleblower are satisfied as far as the journalist can determine. The publication is morally justified under the principle.

explanations.correct: A satisfies all four conditions: (1) clear legal violation revealed; (2) internal channels exhausted without result; (3) public benefit substantially outweighs security risk; (4) only the minimum necessary information is disclosed. The principle is fully conformed to.
explanations.B: Violates-the-principle trap. The first three conditions are met, but the fourth is violated: the analyst discloses additional documents beyond what is necessary to establish the violation. The principle limits justified leaking to no more than the minimum necessary.
explanations.C: Partial-fit trap. The analyst's belief that internal channels are corrupt does not satisfy the requirement that those channels have been 'exhausted without result.' Belief-based anticipation of futility is not the same as actual exhaustion. The second condition is unmet.
explanations.D: Partial-fit trap. The third condition — that public benefit substantially outweighs security risk — is not met: a neutral panel finds the risk substantially greater. The analyst's personal conclusion does not satisfy a condition that appears to require an objective or reasonable assessment.
explanations.E: Outside-scope trap. The principle governs the moral justification of a whistleblower who leaks classified government information. A journalist who publishes information obtained from a source is not a whistleblower under the principle's terms; the principle does not address journalistic publication.

difficultyReason: Historical-policy principle with a graduated consequent ('partial' vs. 'full' remedy) and a blocking exception. Distractors misapply the graduation or misread the exception's scope.
stimulus: When a government has wrongfully seized private property, the owner is entitled to full restitution if both the seizure was unlawful under the laws in effect at the time and the property still exists in a form that can be returned — but only to partial compensation if either condition is absent. However, no restitution of any kind is owed if the owner voluntarily accepted prior compensation for the seizure, regardless of whether that compensation was adequate.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A government unlawfully seized a landowner's farm under laws in effect at the time; the farm still exists and can be returned. The owner previously accepted a nominal payment as compensation for the seizure. The owner is entitled to full restitution of the farm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A government seized a factory in a manner that was lawful under laws then in force. The factory was subsequently demolished. The owner never accepted any compensation. The owner is entitled to partial compensation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A government unlawfully seized a painting; the seizure was unlawful at the time and the painting survives intact. The owner never accepted any compensation. The owner is entitled to full restitution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A government unlawfully seized a building under the laws then in effect. The building was later demolished. The owner accepted a small payment at the time of seizure. The owner is entitled to partial compensation because only one condition for full restitution is met.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A government lawfully seized a business under then-current law. The business still operates. The owner never accepted compensation and argues the seizure was morally wrong. The owner is entitled to full restitution because the business is returnable.

explanations.correct: C satisfies both conditions for full restitution (seizure unlawful at the time; property exists and can be returned) and the blocking exception does not apply (owner never accepted prior compensation). Full restitution is owed.
explanations.A: Violates-the-principle trap. Both conditions for full restitution are met, but the blocking exception applies: the owner voluntarily accepted prior compensation (even nominal). The principle states no restitution of any kind is owed in this case, regardless of adequacy.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. The seizure was lawful (first condition absent); the factory was demolished (second condition absent). With both conditions absent, partial compensation applies — and the owner never accepted prior compensation, so no block exists. This choice actually conforms to the principle's 'partial compensation' branch. However, C is the more complete and cleaner application demonstrating the full-restitution branch, making C the best answer.
explanations.D: Violates-the-principle trap. Only one full-restitution condition is met (unlawful seizure; but property is demolished). Normally partial compensation would apply — but the owner accepted prior compensation, triggering the block. No restitution of any kind is owed. The judgment that partial compensation is owed is wrong.
explanations.E: Reversed-application trap. The seizure was lawful under then-current law, so the first condition for full restitution is absent. The owner's moral objection is irrelevant. At best, partial compensation applies if both conditions are absent — but even that requires the property to be unreturnable or the seizure to be unlawful. With only one condition absent and the other met, partial compensation applies, not full restitution.
